title: Maximum Elegance of a K-Length Subsequence
statement:
You are given an array `items` of length `n`, where `items[i] = [profit_i, category_i]`, and an integer `k`. Choose a subsequence of exactly `k` items, that is, any `k` items at different indices (their order does not affect the score).

The **elegance** of a choice is the sum of its profits plus the square of the number of distinct categories it contains. Return the largest elegance that any choice of exactly `k` items can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every set of `k` items is exponential. Instead, start from the most profitable choice, the top `k` profits, and ask how it could improve. Taking any item out to add one with lower profit only helps if the new item brings a **category not yet chosen**, raising the bonus from `d²` to `(d + 1)²`. And the item to take out must be a **duplicate** (its category appears again in the choice), otherwise a category is lost and nothing is gained. Among duplicates, the cheapest one costs least. Processing the remaining items in falling profit order, each new category is added at the best price available, so checking the score after every swap covers every useful number of distinct categories.

## Approach

1. Sort `items` by profit, largest first.
2. Take the first `k`: add each `profit` to `total`. A category seen for the first time goes into `seen`; otherwise push the profit onto `duplicates`. Because profits fall, the top of `duplicates` is always the cheapest duplicate.
3. Set `best = total + seen.size²`.
4. Scan the remaining items. Stop when `duplicates` is empty (no item can be given up), and skip items whose category is already in `seen`.
5. Otherwise swap: `total += profit - duplicates.pop()`, add the category, and update `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted, `items = [[10,1],[5,1],[3,2]]` and `k = 2`. The first two give `total = 15`, `seen = {1}` and `duplicates = [5]`, so `best = 15 + 1 = 16`. Item `[3,2]` has a new category: `total = 15 + 3 - 5 = 13`, `seen = {1, 2}`, and `13 + 4 = 17` beats 16. The answer is `17`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scans are O(n).
- Space: O(n) for `seen` and `duplicates`.

## Pitfalls

- A swap can lower the score now and raise it later, so keep `best` separately instead of stopping at the first drop.
- Never remove the only item of a category: only true duplicates may be swapped out.
- Use each new category once: a second item of an already-added category is skipped.
- Totals reach about 10^14, beyond 32-bit integers (`long` in Java and C).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | categories in the current choice |
| `duplicates` | profits of chosen items whose category was already present, cheapest on top |
| `total` | sum of profits of the current choice |
| `best` | highest elegance found so far |
| `profit`, `category` | the item being considered |

narration.2: Sort by profit, largest first, so the first k items are the most profitable choice.
narration.6: Start with the k most profitable items.
narration.8: Every chosen item adds its profit.
narration.9: Its category is already in the choice...
narration.10: ...so this item is a duplicate that could later be given up; it is the cheapest so far.
narration.12: A first item of its category adds a distinct category.
narration.15: Score the starting choice: profits plus distinct categories squared.
narration.16: Consider the remaining items from most to least profitable.
narration.18: With no duplicates left, no swap can keep every category, so stop.
narration.21: An item of a category already chosen adds nothing new.
narration.24: Swap out the cheapest duplicate for this item, changing the profit by the difference.
narration.25: The new category raises the distinct count.
narration.26: Keep the best score among all the choices tried.
